# admin-tools

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D4 Backend & APIs (BE)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Django admin documentation — https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/4.2/ref/contrib/admin/ ; Stripe, PCI compliance guidance (SAQ A scope, hosted card collection) — https://stripe.com/guides/pci-compliance
- **Depends on:** rbac, backend-auth, api-building
- **Feeds into:** user-reporting, incident-response

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** staff need to operate the product — look up users, correct data, refund, moderate, configure — through a surface that is safer than a database console and more honest than a demo panel.
- **Do NOT use when:** the surface is for end users; that is the product itself. Do not build admin actions as a parallel write path around the domain services — admin tooling rides the same service layer, or it will diverge from the product it operates.

## Rules

1. **BE-161 — Same service layer.** Admin actions call the same domain services users hit, so validation, authorization, and side effects match the product. There is no admin-only write path into the database.
2. **BE-162 — Mutations persist and propagate.** An admin change is done only when it survives reload and is visible on every user-facing surface it affects. A confirmation toast is not evidence.
3. **BE-163 — Dashboards compute live.** Every figure on an admin dashboard is computed from current records at view time, or on a stated refresh cycle. No fixture or constant renders as a metric.
4. **BE-164 — Audit record on every mutation.** Each admin mutation writes actor, action, target, before/after values, and timestamp — as part of the action, not as a later courtesy.
5. **BE-165 — Scoped staff roles.** Staff access is least-privilege by role and enforced server-side (see rbac). A read-only role cannot mutate by calling the endpoint directly.
6. **BE-166 — Destructive actions are two-step.** Refunds, bans, and data corrections are prepared, shown for confirmation with their effect stated, then executed. Where the domain allows, they are reversible or compensatable.
7. **BE-167 — Card data never renders.** Admin screens show at most card brand + last 4, taken from the provider's card object. A full PAN is never displayed, stored, or logged; card collection stays with the provider (SAQ A scope).
8. **BE-168 — Stricter staff sessions.** Admin sessions idle out faster than user sessions, and high-impact actions require re-authentication at the moment of execution.
9. **BE-169 — Repeated fixes become tools.** If support performs the same manual fix twice, it becomes an admin tool with validation and an audit trail. Raw SQL against production is not an operating procedure.
10. **BE-170 — A separate, staff-authenticated surface.** The admin app authenticates staff independently of the user app. A user session, however privileged in the product, opens nothing here.

## BAN list

- **BAN-BE-081 — The save-nothing panel.** Banned: an admin edit that shows "Saved" while writing nothing, or writing only to local component state. Defeats: DET-FAKE-010. Instead: route the edit through the domain service and confirm only after the persisted value is read back (BE-162). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-BE-082 — The fixture dashboard.** Banned: dashboard metrics rendered from constants or seed fixtures presented as live figures. Defeats: DET-FAKE-004. Instead: compute from live records; a metric that cannot be computed displays "unavailable", never an invented number. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-BE-083 — Full PAN on screen or in logs.** Banned: rendering, storing, or logging a full card number anywhere in admin tooling. Defeats: DET-CODE-029. Instead: store and display only brand + last 4 from the provider's card object, and redact card-shaped strings in logs. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-BE-084 — Hidden-URL access control.** Banned: protecting admin routes only by an unlinked URL, or by a client-side role check, while the endpoints accept ordinary user sessions. Defeats: DET-FAKE-021. Instead: separate staff authentication plus a server-side role check on every admin route (BE-165, BE-170). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-BE-081 — Limited-role denial test.** Verifies: BE-165. Check: automated — authenticate as the read-only staff role and attempt a mutation (price change, refund) through the UI and by direct API call. Pass: both refused server-side with 403 and no state change. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-BE-082 — Audit-completeness test.** Verifies: BE-164. Check: automated — perform a test refund in staging, then query the audit log. Shape-adapted form: where the product has no refunds (or no payments at all), perform instead the most consequential audited staff mutation the product does have — a record deletion, a role or permission change, a status override — and query the audit log for that mutation; the evidence bar is identical. Pass: a record exists with actor, action, target, before/after values, and timestamp. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-BE-083 — PAN-pattern scan.** Verifies: BE-167. Check: automated — run a Luhn-validated card-number pattern scan over admin templates, rendered staging pages, and application logs. Pass: zero full-PAN matches; brand + last-4 formats pass. Fail: block shipment and purge the contaminated log. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-BE-084 — Persistence round-trip.** Verifies: BE-161, BE-162. Check: automated — change a product price as staff, reload the admin view, then fetch the public product page as an anonymous visitor. Shape-adapted form: where the product has no prices or no public page, change any staff-editable record instead and compare the admin view against the surface that record is actually read from — the end-user view, the API response, or the next reader's view — with the same three-way agreement required. Pass: all three views agree on the new price (or, under the shape-adapted form, on the changed record). Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- Admin actions ride the same services users hit.
- If it didn't persist and propagate, it didn't happen.
- Every mutation writes its audit record.
- Brand + last 4 is all a screen may ever show.
- A fix done twice by hand becomes a tool.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every admin mutation round-trips: reload and the read surface agree (G-BE-084).
- [ ] The read-only staff role is refused mutations server-side (G-BE-081).
- [ ] A test refund (or the shape-adapted audited mutation) produced a complete audit record (G-BE-082).
- [ ] The PAN scan over pages and logs is clean (G-BE-083).
- [ ] Destructive actions are two-step, with the effect shown before execution (BE-166).
- [ ] Staff sessions time out faster than user sessions; high-impact actions re-authenticate (BE-168).
- [ ] No admin handler writes the database outside the service layer (BE-161).

# api-building

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D4 Backend & APIs (BE)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** OpenAPI Specification v3.1.0 — https://spec.openapis.org/oas/v3.1.0 ; Stripe, "Idempotent requests" — https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests ; PROJECT_ANATOMY.md, "API implementation"
- **Depends on:** api-architecture, validation, error-handling
- **Feeds into:** sdk-design, admin-tools, payments

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** implementing or reviewing any HTTP endpoint that reads or writes server state — the handler pipeline, idempotency, transactions, and response shaping for a route all live here.
- **Do NOT use when:** the question is what the API should look like (rest-conventions owns shape and naming), how a specific payload is validated (validation), or how errors are formatted in depth (error-handling). This skill assumes those decisions exist and builds handlers that honor them.

## Rules

1. **BE-001 — One handler pipeline.** Every handler runs in this order: authenticate → authorize (object-level) → validate against the schema → run the domain operation → serialize through the response mapper. No step is skipped or reordered.
2. **BE-002 — Persistence is the definition of done.** A write endpoint is done only when its effect survives a reload and is visible from a second session or client. A 200/201 response is not evidence of an effect.
3. **BE-003 — The server recomputes trusted values.** Amounts, prices, roles, and owner IDs are never taken from the request; they are looked up or recomputed server-side from the authenticated identity and stored data.
4. **BE-004 — The database arbitrates races.** Check-then-act sequences (stock, uniqueness, balance) run inside a transaction or behind a unique constraint. Application-level "check then write" without one is a defect.
5. **BE-005 — Idempotency keys on non-replayable writes.** POSTs that create orders, take payments, or send messages accept an `Idempotency-Key`: the server stores the key with a hash of the request and the first response, replays the stored response on retry, and rejects reuse of the key with a different body.
6. **BE-006 — Two exits only.** Every handler ends in the success serializer or the problem-details error path. There is no third response shape — no ad-hoc JSON, no plain-text errors, no 200-with-error.
7. **BE-007 — Long work returns 202.** Work that depends on a slow or third-party operation returns `202` with a status resource and continues as a background job (queues-jobs). The request never blocks on a provider.
8. **BE-008 — Serializers whitelist contract fields.** Responses are built by a mapper that exposes only the fields in the OpenAPI contract. Raw database rows or ORM entities are never serialized directly.
9. **BE-009 — The contract is the source of truth.** The OpenAPI description is written or updated with the endpoint, and contract tests run against the running service in CI. Implementation and contract may not drift silently.
10. **BE-010 — Multi-record writes are atomic.** A handler that changes more than one record commits all of them or none of them in a single transaction. A partial write left behind by an error is a defect.

## BAN list

- **BAN-BE-001 — Stub handler shipped as an endpoint.** Banned: a route whose body returns a constant, a fixture, or a generated ID without performing the operation, while callers treat it as done. Defeats: DET-CODE-003. Instead: implement the real write path through the pipeline (BE-001), or keep the route unregistered until it is real. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-BE-002 — Success response with no persisted effect.** Banned: a handler that reports success while discarding the submission — no record created, nothing retrievable afterward. Defeats: DET-FAKE-015. Instead: persist the submission in the same request and make it retrievable by its owner. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-BE-003 — Client-supplied role or owner trusted.** Banned: authorizing or scoping a write using a role, owner ID, or tenant ID taken from the request body, query, or headers. Defeats: DET-FAKE-021. Instead: derive ownership from the authenticated session server-side (BE-003) and authorize the object on every request. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-BE-004 — Check-then-act without a constraint.** Banned: reading a value (stock, balance, existence) and then writing based on it, with no transaction, lock, unique constraint, or atomic update between the read and the write. Defeats: DET-CODE-030. Instead: decrement atomically (`UPDATE … WHERE stock > 0` and check affected rows) or transact with a uniqueness constraint (BE-004). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-BE-001 — Contract test suite.** Verifies: BE-001, BE-009. Check: automated — run the contract test suite against the running service in CI; every endpoint in the OpenAPI document is exercised for shape, status codes, and error format. Pass: 100% of contract tests green. Fail: block merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-BE-002 — Persistence test per write endpoint.** Verifies: BE-002. Check: automated — for each write endpoint, perform the write, reload, and re-read the resource from a second session; assert the effect is present and identical. Pass: every write endpoint's effect survives and is visible cross-session. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-BE-003 — Duplicate-submit test.** Verifies: BE-004, BE-005. Check: automated — submit the same create request twice concurrently with one idempotency key, and twice with no key where the schema forbids duplicates; assert exactly one record and one effect. Pass: single effect in both runs. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-BE-004 — Trusted-value audit.** Verifies: BE-003. Check: automated grep plus review — search handlers for request-derived fields named `amount`, `price`, `total`, `role`, `ownerId`, or `tenantId` reaching a write without a server-side lookup; hand-check every hit. Pass: zero unexamined hits. Fail: warn, and fix before the endpoint ships. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- Authenticate, authorize, validate, transact, serialize — in that order.
- A response is not an effect; persistence is the definition of done.
- The client proposes; the server recomputes.
- Retries must be safe: idempotency keys on every non-replayable write.
- Two exits only: the serializer or problem details.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every handler follows the BE-001 pipeline with no skipped step.
- [ ] Every write endpoint passes its persistence test (G-BE-002).
- [ ] No trusted value (amount, price, role, owner) is taken from the request (G-BE-004).
- [ ] Non-replayable POSTs accept and honor `Idempotency-Key` (G-BE-003).
- [ ] Check-then-act paths run in a transaction or behind a constraint (BE-004).
- [ ] Responses serialize only contract fields (BE-008).
- [ ] Contract tests are green against the running service (G-BE-001).

# backend-auth

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D4 Backend & APIs (BE)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet — https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Session_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html ; PROJECT_ANATOMY.md, "Authentication and authorization implementation"
- **Depends on:** secrets-management, rate-limiting
- **Feeds into:** rbac, oauth-sso, session-security

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** implementing or reviewing signup, login (by password, passkey/WebAuthn, or a delegated flow), logout, session handling, or password reset for any client — anywhere the system must prove who a caller is before trusting a request. Whatever the proof method, the session it produces obeys this skill's rules.
- **Do NOT use when:** deciding what an authenticated user may do (rbac), hardening auth against advanced attacks in depth (auth-hardening), or running OAuth/OIDC provider flows (oauth-sso — though the session those flows produce obeys this skill's rules). This skill owns identity proof and the session lifecycle.

## Rules

1. **BE-101 — Server-side proof on every request.** Authentication is verified by the server on each protected request. Client state — a storage flag, a hidden route, a client-sent role — is never evidence of authentication.
2. **BE-102 — Passwords are hashed, memory-hard, salted.** Passwords are stored only as hashes from a vetted memory-hard algorithm (Argon2id/bcrypt class) with a per-user salt. Plaintext storage, reversible encryption, and fast hashes (MD5/SHA-1/plain SHA-2) are defects.
3. **BE-103 — Sessions are server-issued and cookie-carried.** A session is a high-entropy opaque ID (or a signed token with server-side revocation), issued at login and carried in a `Secure` + `HttpOnly` + `SameSite` cookie for browser clients.
4. **BE-104 — Rotation on authentication and privilege change.** The session ID is rotated at login and whenever privilege changes; the previous ID stops working immediately.
5. **BE-105 — Expiry is enforced server-side.** Logout, idle timeout, and absolute timeout all invalidate the session on the server. A client deleting its cookie is not a logout.
6. **BE-106 — Signup is not done until login works.** Signup completes only when the account record exists, the password is hashed per BE-102, and a login with the new credentials from a clean session succeeds.
7. **BE-107 — Reset is a credential change.** A reset uses a single-use, expiring token; completing it changes the stored credential and revokes all existing sessions. The old password must stop working.
8. **BE-108 — No account enumeration.** Failed-login responses are identical in body and status for an unknown account and a wrong password, and signup/reset messaging never confirms whether an account exists.
9. **BE-109 — Auth endpoints are rate-limited.** Login, signup, and reset endpoints carry per-account and per-IP limits (mechanics in rate-limiting), independent of the API's general budget.
10. **BE-110 — Credentials never leak into artifacts.** Passwords, session IDs, and reset tokens never appear in URLs, logs, error responses, or analytics events.
11. **BE-111 — Delegated login changes nothing.** A session produced by an OAuth/OIDC flow (oauth-sso) obeys BE-103 through BE-105 identically — same cookie attributes, rotation, and server-side expiry.

## BAN list

- **BAN-BE-051 — Any-password login.** Banned: a login that accepts any password, one hardcoded credential, or a credential check performed only in client code. Defeats: DET-FAKE-001. Instead: verify credentials server-side against the stored hash (BE-101, BE-102) and reject wrong passwords with the generic error (BE-108). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-BE-052 — Session that is only a flag.** Banned: post-login state stored as a `localStorage` boolean or in-memory variable, with protected data served on the client's say-so. Defeats: DET-FAKE-002. Instead: issue a server-side session in a `Secure` + `HttpOnly` cookie and enforce it on every request (BE-101, BE-103). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-BE-053 — Signup that registers nothing.** Banned: a signup flow that shows success while creating no account record — data discarded, or kept only in the browser. Defeats: DET-FAKE-003. Instead: write the account with its hashed password, then prove it — a clean-session login with the new credentials succeeds before signup is called done (BE-106). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-BE-054 — Reset that resets nothing.** Banned: a forgot-password flow whose token is unchecked, reusable, or disconnected from the credential store, so the "reset" succeeds and the old password keeps working. Defeats: DET-FAKE-020. Instead: single-use expiring token; on use, replace the hash and revoke all sessions (BE-107). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-BE-055 — Plaintext or fast-hash password storage.** Banned: storing passwords in plaintext, reversibly encrypted, or hashed with a fast unsalted algorithm. Defeats: DET-CODE-020 (nearest match — no DET parameter names this exact signal). Instead: hash with a memory-hard algorithm and a per-user salt (BE-102), and verify storage with G-BE-052. Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-BE-051 — Auth test pack.** Verifies: BE-101, BE-103, BE-105. Check: automated — in CI, run the pack against a running instance: wrong password is rejected; a real session survives a reload; after logout the same session ID is refused server-side; a direct API call with no credentials returns `401`. Pass: all four behaviors hold. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-BE-052 — Credential-store inspection.** Verifies: BE-102. Check: automated query plus manual review — select the password column for all users; assert every value matches the approved hash format, salts are unique per user, and no value equals or contains its plaintext. Pass: 100% conforming hashes, zero plaintext. Fail: block shipment and treat any plaintext find as an incident. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-BE-053 — Reset drill.** Verifies: BE-107. Check: automated — on a test account, request a reset, complete it, then assert: the old password fails, the new password works from a clean session, the token cannot be reused, and sessions opened before the reset are rejected. Pass: all four assertions hold. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-BE-054 — Enumeration probe.** Verifies: BE-108. Check: automated — submit failed logins for an existing account with a wrong password and for a nonexistent account; compare status, body, and response shape. Pass: responses are indistinguishable. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- Client state is never evidence; the server proves identity on every request.
- Hash memory-hard and salted — plaintext and fast hashes are defects.
- Logout, idle, and absolute expiry all kill the session server-side.
- Reset changes the credential and revokes every session.
- Unknown user and wrong password get the same answer.

## Checklist

- [ ] Wrong password is rejected and a real session survives reload (G-BE-051).
- [ ] Every stored password is a salted memory-hard hash; zero plaintext (G-BE-052).
- [ ] Sessions ride in Secure + HttpOnly + SameSite cookies and rotate on login and privilege change (BE-103, BE-104).
- [ ] Logout invalidates the session server-side, not just the cookie (BE-105).
- [ ] Signup is proven by a clean-session login with the new credentials (BE-106).
- [ ] The reset drill passes: old password dead, token single-use, prior sessions revoked (G-BE-053).
- [ ] Login failures are indistinguishable for unknown vs. existing accounts (G-BE-054).
- [ ] No password, session ID, or reset token appears in any URL or log (BE-110).

# error-handling

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D4 Backend & APIs (BE)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** RFC 9457 (Problem Details for HTTP APIs), https://ftp.kaist.ac.kr/rfc/rfc9457.html ; OWASP Error Handling Cheat Sheet, https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Error_Handling_Cheat_Sheet.html
- **Depends on:** api-building, validation
- **Feeds into:** error-tracking (D12), api-documentation, sdk-design

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** designing how any backend reports failure — error responses, exception translation, logging of errors, status-code choice — or auditing an API whose failures all look the same or leak internals.
- **Do NOT use when:** the question is which status code a successful or conventional response carries in general (rest-conventions owns the convention sheet; this skill owns the failure path), or frontend display of errors (D3's ui-states).

## Rules

1. **BE-281 — One exit path.** Every handler ends in exactly one of two exits: the success serializer or the single global error handler. No handler formats its own error response.
2. **BE-282 — Problem details only.** Client-facing errors are RFC 9457 problem details — `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`, `instance` — with extension members for per-field validation errors and a correlation ID. No other error shape exists in the API.
3. **BE-283 — Typed errors inside.** Domain code raises typed errors that carry a problem type. Raw library and framework exceptions are translated at the boundary into those types, never formatted ad hoc per handler.
4. **BE-284 — No internals out.** A response never contains a stack trace, SQL fragment, table or column name, file path, framework version, or a downstream provider's raw payload.
5. **BE-285 — Full truth inside.** The complete exception, request context, and the same correlation ID the client received are written to structured logs and error tracking. What the client must not see, the operator must.
6. **BE-286 — Classified by who can fix it.** Every error class is one of: caller-fixable (4xx with actionable detail), conflict (409/412), dependency failure (502/503 with retry guidance), or ours (500, alerted). The classification decides the status and the detail level.
7. **BE-287 — No swallowed errors.** An error is handled, translated, or propagated. Empty catches and catch-log-continue-as-if-success are forbidden; best-effort cleanup is the only exception, and it carries a comment stating why failure is safe.
8. **BE-288 — Fail closed.** An error inside an authorization, validation, or payment step denies the operation. No error path defaults to allow, skip, or proceed.
9. **BE-289 — Distinct signals.** Different failures produce different problem types and messages a client can act on. One generic message reused for every failure is forbidden.
10. **BE-290 — Every 5xx is observable.** Each 5xx response corresponds to a log record and a metric carrying the same correlation ID. A 5xx nobody can find afterward is a defect in this skill, not bad luck.

## BAN list

- **BAN-BE-141 — The empty catch.** Banned: catch blocks that are empty, comment-only, or log the error and continue as if the operation succeeded. Defeats: DET-CODE-005. Instead: translate the failure into a typed error or propagate it (BE-283, BE-287). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-BE-142 — One message for everything.** Banned: returning the same generic error body for validation failures, missing records, and outages alike. Defeats: DET-CODE-022. Instead: classified problem details, distinct per failure class (BE-286, BE-289). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-BE-143 — The leaking error.** Banned: error responses containing stack traces, SQL, internal paths, or provider payloads. Defeats: DET-CODE-020. Instead: a generic 500 problem to the client, the full exception to the logs (BE-284, BE-285). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-BE-144 — Fail-open on error.** Banned: an exception inside an authorization or validation check causing the request to be allowed. Defeats: DET-FAKE-021. Instead: deny the operation on any check error (BE-288). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-BE-145 — The naked boundary call.** Banned: network, filesystem, or database calls with no timeout and no defined failure path. Defeats: DET-CODE-006. Instead: timeout plus a typed failure translated into a classified problem (BE-283, BE-286). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-BE-141 — Error-shape contract test.** Verifies: BE-282, BE-284, BE-289. Check: automated suite that forces each error class (validation, not-found, conflict, dependency down, unexpected) and asserts the problem-details shape, the correct status, distinct `type` values, and the absence of internal markers (stack frames, SQL keywords, absolute paths) in every body. Pass: all assertions hold. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-BE-142 — Negative-path fuzz run.** Verifies: BE-281, BE-287. Check: automated — fuzz and negative inputs across endpoints; assert no unhandled-exception response (framework error page, empty 500, dropped connection) ever reaches a client. Pass: zero unhandled responses. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-BE-143 — Swallow scan.** Verifies: BE-287. Check: automated lint/grep for empty catch blocks and catch blocks whose only action is a log call followed by a success flow; allowlisted best-effort cleanup must carry its justifying comment. Pass: zero unexplained hits. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-BE-144 — Correlation trace.** Verifies: BE-285, BE-290. Check: manual step in staging — trigger a 500, take the correlation ID from the response body, and locate the full exception in the logs or error tracking under that ID. Pass: found, complete, same ID. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- Two exits only: success serializer or the one error handler.
- Problem details out, full exception in — same correlation ID.
- Classify by who can fix it; that decides status and detail.
- Nothing is swallowed; nothing fails open.
- Different failures get different signals.

## Checklist

- [ ] All error responses are problem details from the single handler (BE-281, BE-282).
- [ ] Error-shape contract test green, no internal markers in any body (G-BE-141).
- [ ] Fuzz run produced zero unhandled-exception responses (G-BE-142).
- [ ] Swallow scan clean or every hit justified in a comment (G-BE-143).
- [ ] A staging 500 traces from response correlation ID to full log record (G-BE-144).
- [ ] Security and validation checks deny on error (BE-288).
- [ ] Every 5xx emits a log record and a metric with its correlation ID (BE-290).

# feature-flags

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D4 Backend & APIs (BE)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Pete Hodgson, "Feature Toggles" — https://martinfowler.com/articles/feature-toggles.html ; LaunchDarkly, "Kill switches, progressive rollouts, and user targeting" — https://LaunchDarkly.com/blog/kill-switches-progressive-rollouts-user-targeting/
- **Depends on:** api-building
- **Feeds into:** experimentation-platform, ci-cd

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** shipping a risky path before it is proven, rolling a change out gradually, running an experiment, or needing a kill path for a feature in production — any behavior that must change without a redeploy.
- **Do NOT use when:** the behavior is a permission (rbac owns who may do something; a flag may hide a feature, never authorize it), a permanent product configuration value (that is settings, not a flag), or a substitute for finishing the work — a flag is not a way to merge a stub.

## Rules

1. **BE-061 — Registry before code.** A flag exists in the central registry — key, owner, type, safe default, expiry date — before any code references its key. A key invented at the keyboard does not ship.
2. **BE-062 — Every flag has a type.** Each flag is typed release, experiment, ops, or permissioning (the Fowler taxonomy). Type determines expected lifetime: release flags live days, experiment flags live until their end date, ops flags are reviewed on a schedule.
3. **BE-063 — The default is the safe value.** If the flag service is unreachable or the key is unknown, evaluation returns the flag's safe default — for a release flag, the old behavior. A flag outage must never enable the unproven path.
4. **BE-064 — One evaluation path.** Flags are evaluated server-side through a single toggle router. Feature code asks the router; it never calls a flag SDK directly, and client code never decides behavior the server will not re-check.
5. **BE-065 — Bucketing is deterministic.** Percentage rollouts assign users by hashing a stable key (flag key + user ID). The same user gets the same variant on every request, device, and service — never a coin flip per request.
6. **BE-066 — The off path is a tested product path.** The flag-off behavior is built, tested, and monitored like the flag-on behavior. Every release flag has a kill path that takes effect without a redeploy.
7. **BE-067 — Expiry is enforced, removal is done.** A flag past its expiry date fails review. When a release rollout completes, the flag and the dead branch are removed in the same work — removal is part of the feature's definition of done.
8. **BE-068 — Flags never replace authorization.** A flag may control visibility or rollout of a feature; the API still enforces who may use it on every request, flag or no flag.
9. **BE-069 — Flag changes are audited like deploys.** Every production flag change records actor, timestamp, previous and new value, and reason, in a log that survives the flag's removal.
10. **BE-070 — Experiments are pre-registered.** An experiment flag is created only with a hypothesis, a primary metric, and an end date recorded (with experimentation-platform). A flag created "to see what happens" is not an experiment.

## BAN list

- **BAN-BE-031 — The permanent flag.** Banned: a flag that will never be removed — `if (true)` in flag's clothing, a renamed leftover (`new_checkout_v2_final`), or a release flag still gating code two releases after rollout completed. Defeats: DET-CODE-001. Instead: when rollout completes, delete the flag, the registry entry, and the dead branch in the same change (BE-067). Severity: WARN.
- **BAN-BE-032 — Flag as the only permission check.** Banned: protecting an operation by hiding it behind a flag or a UI toggle while the endpoint itself performs no authorization. Defeats: DET-FAKE-021. Instead: keep the flag for visibility if useful, and enforce the role check server-side on the endpoint (BE-068, rbac). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-BE-033 — Same flag, different defaults.** Banned: one flag key carrying different default values in different services or environments, so the system has no single answer to "is it on?" Defeats: DET-CODE-032. Instead: one registry entry with one safe default; environments override the value explicitly, never the default (BE-061, BE-063). Severity: WARN.
- **BAN-BE-034 — The zombie flag.** Banned: flag keys that no code references anymore, left in the registry and in configuration after their feature shipped or was cut. Defeats: DET-CODE-002. Instead: removing a feature removes its flag everywhere; the registry-vs-codebase diff (G-BE-031) flags orphans in both directions. Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-BE-031 — Registry-vs-codebase diff.** Verifies: BE-061, BE-067. Check: automated — extract every flag key referenced in code and diff against the registry; assert each referenced key exists with an owner and an unexpired date, and each registry entry is referenced by code. Pass: zero orphans in either direction, zero expired flags. Fail: block merge. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-BE-032 — Staging flip test.** Verifies: BE-063, BE-066. Check: automated — in staging, turn one release flag off and confirm the feature disappears with no redeploy and the fallback path renders and functions; turn it back on and confirm restoration. Pass: both directions clean. Fail: block the rollout. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-BE-033 — Bucketing stability test.** Verifies: BE-065. Check: automated — evaluate one percentage-rollout flag 100 times for each of a sample of user keys across two services; assert a stable variant per user and a distribution within tolerance of the configured percentage. Pass: zero flickers, distribution in tolerance. Fail: block the rollout. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-BE-034 — Flag-change audit review.** Verifies: BE-069. Check: manual — review the period's production flag changes; each must carry actor, reason, and previous/new values. Pass: 100% of changes fully recorded. Fail: warn, and complete the record before the next release. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- Registry before code: owner, type, safe default, expiry.
- The default is the safe value — an outage never enables the new path.
- Same user, same variant, every time.
- The off path is a product path; test it like one.
- A finished rollout deletes the flag, not just flips it.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every flag key in code exists in the registry with owner, type, default, and unexpired date (G-BE-031).
- [ ] Rollouts bucket deterministically on a stable user key (G-BE-033).
- [ ] The flag-off path is tested and the kill path works without a redeploy (G-BE-032).
- [ ] No flag is the only enforcement of a permission (BE-068).
- [ ] Completed rollouts have their flag and dead branch removed (BE-067).
- [ ] Production flag changes in the period are fully audit-logged (G-BE-034).
- [ ] Experiment flags carry a hypothesis, metric, and end date (BE-070).

# file-uploads

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D4 Backend & APIs (BE)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet, https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/File_Upload_Cheat_Sheet.html ; AWS S3 presigned URLs, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
- **Depends on:** backend-auth, validation, queues-jobs
- **Feeds into:** media-processing, admin-tools

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** users upload files of any kind — avatars, documents, attachments, imports — or when reviewing an existing upload flow for safety and honesty.
- **Do NOT use when:** the file never leaves the server that generated it (server-side exports are api-building plus data-access), or for what happens to media after upload — derivatives and transcodes are media-processing.

## Rules

1. **BE-221 — Presigned direct upload.** The app server authenticates the user, registers the upload intent, and issues a short-lived presigned URL; bytes flow from the client directly to private object storage. The database stores metadata and the object key only, never file contents.
2. **BE-222 — Completion means stored.** An upload is complete only when the object exists in storage (verified by a storage existence check) and the metadata row points at its key. A client-side preview or progress bar is never evidence of completion.
3. **BE-223 — Layered validation.** Every upload passes, in order: authenticated user, size cap, extension allowlist checked on the decoded filename, and content signature sniffing. The client-supplied Content-Type is never trusted as evidence of type.
4. **BE-224 — Generated stored names.** Stored object names are server-generated (UUID or equivalent). The original filename is kept as display metadata only and never reaches a filesystem path or object key.
5. **BE-225 — Private by default.** Buckets and storage containers are private. Downloads are authorized per request and served through a signed URL or a handler that maps an opaque ID to the object after an authorization check.
6. **BE-226 — Inert where served.** Uploads are stored outside any executable path and served with a safe Content-Type and `Content-Disposition`; user content is never rendered as active content from the application's own origin.
7. **BE-227 — Limits at the storage layer.** Size and type limits are encoded in the presigned policy as well as enforced in code, so a forged direct upload that bypasses the application still fails at storage.
8. **BE-228 — Scan before visible.** A malware scan completes before an uploaded file becomes visible or downloadable to anyone, including the uploader's audience. Unscanned files stay in a quarantined state.
9. **BE-229 — Orphan reaping.** Uploads never attached to a record are reaped by a scheduled job on a documented threshold; abandoned bytes are not kept forever.
10. **BE-230 — State is read, not assumed.** Upload states shown anywhere (pending, stored, scanned, failed) are read from the storage and metadata records, never inferred from what the client claims happened.

## BAN list

- **BAN-BE-111 — The discarding upload.** Banned: an upload flow that previews the file locally and reports success without storing it server-side. Defeats: DET-FAKE-012. Instead: presigned upload to storage plus a metadata row, complete only when the object exists (BE-221, BE-222). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-BE-112 — Content-Type trust.** Banned: accepting a file because the client-supplied Content-Type or extension claims a safe type, with no signature sniffing. Defeats: DET-CODE-019. Instead: allowlist the extension on the decoded name and sniff the content signature (BE-223). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-BE-113 — User-named public storage.** Banned: storing uploads under the original filename in a public bucket or a web-served executable folder. Defeats: DET-CODE-020. Instead: generated names in a private bucket, downloads via signed URL (BE-224, BE-225). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-BE-114 — The uncapped upload.** Banned: an upload path with no size limit enforced in code and in the presigned policy. Defeats: DET-CODE-033. Instead: enforce the cap at both layers (BE-227). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-BE-111 — Upload round-trip.** Verifies: BE-221, BE-222, BE-225. Check: automated script — upload a uniquely named file through the real flow, HEAD the bucket object, assert the metadata row holds the key and no contents, assert an unauthenticated GET is denied, and assert the signed URL stops working after expiry. Pass: all assertions hold. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-BE-112 — Hostile-file pack.** Verifies: BE-223, BE-227. Check: automated test pack — double extension, spoofed Content-Type, oversized file, and a polyglot file are each submitted; assert every one is rejected. Pass: zero accepted. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-BE-113 — Path and bucket scan.** Verifies: BE-224, BE-225, BE-226. Check: automated — grep the codebase for original-filename use in path or key construction, and scan storage configuration for public-read policies. Pass: no hits. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-BE-114 — Quarantine and reaper review.** Verifies: BE-228, BE-229. Check: manual step in staging — upload a file, confirm it is not downloadable before its scan completes, then inspect the reaper job's log and confirm orphans past the threshold are gone. Pass: both confirmed. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- Bytes go client → storage directly; the app only authorizes and registers.
- Complete means the object exists and the row points at it.
- Never trust the client's Content-Type; sniff the signature.
- Stored names are generated; original names are display metadata.
- Private bucket, signed downloads, scan before visible.

## Checklist

- [ ] Presigned flow in place; database holds metadata and key only (BE-221).
- [ ] Completion verified against storage, not the client's progress bar (BE-222).
- [ ] Layered validation passes the hostile-file pack (G-BE-112).
- [ ] No original filename reaches a path or key; bucket is private (G-BE-113).
- [ ] Size and type limits enforced in the presigned policy too (BE-227).
- [ ] Unscanned files are not downloadable; orphans are reaped (G-BE-114).
- [ ] Upload round-trip gate green (G-BE-111).

<!-- generated from skills/backend/media-processing/SKILL.md (bundle form) -->

# media-processing

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D4 Backend & APIs (BE)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet (image re-encoding, parser-exploit and decompression threats), https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/File_Upload_Cheat_Sheet.html
- **Depends on:** file-uploads, queues-jobs
- **Feeds into:** api-building, admin-tools

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** uploaded media must be transformed before use — thumbnails, image re-encoding, video transcodes, waveform/OCR/metadata extraction — or when an asset pipeline's states and failures need to be made honest.
- **Do NOT use when:** the work is accepting and storing the upload itself (file-uploads), or generic background-job mechanics unrelated to media (queues-jobs).

## Rules

1. **BE-241 — Off the request path.** All processing runs as queued jobs. The upload request returns once the asset is registered in a quarantine state; it never waits for a thumbnail, transcode, or extraction to finish.
2. **BE-242 — Quarantine until processed.** An asset is not publishable until its processing job has succeeded and produced the normalized master and required derivatives. Quarantined assets are not served to end users.
3. **BE-243 — Re-encode images.** Images are decoded and re-encoded into an allowed format. Re-encoding is also the sanitation step: embedded payloads and metadata not meant to ship do not survive it.
4. **BE-244 — Resource limits.** Processing runs with explicit time, memory, and pixel/frame caps. Inputs that exceed the caps are rejected as a class; they are never attempted "to see if it works."
5. **BE-245 — Fixed rendition ladder.** Video transcodes target a fixed, documented ladder of renditions for adaptive delivery through the CDN. Renditions are not invented per upload.
6. **BE-246 — Recipe provenance.** Every derivative records its source object, the recipe version that produced it, and its status. A derivative whose origin cannot be stated is treated as corrupt.
7. **BE-247 — Honest failure.** A failed job leaves the asset in a visible failed state with a retry path. The raw original is never silently served in place of the derivatives that failed to appear.
8. **BE-248 — State from the job record.** User-visible state (processing, ready, failed) is read from real job state. No timer, delay, or client-side guess may stand in for it.
9. **BE-249 — Metadata by policy.** EXIF location data is stripped from user photos by default. Handling of other document and media metadata is set per product in writing, not inherited from a library default.
10. **BE-250 — Regenerable derivatives.** The stored original plus its recipe must be able to reproduce every served rendition. Reprocessing after a recipe change is a batch job over the provenance records, not a manual hunt.

## BAN list

- **BAN-BE-121 — The silent fallback to raw.** Banned: serving the unprocessed original when processing fails, with no visible failure state. Defeats: DET-CODE-005. Instead: the asset stays visibly failed with a retry path (BE-247). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-BE-122 — Unbounded processing.** Banned: decoding or transcoding user media with no time, memory, or pixel/frame caps. Defeats: DET-CODE-033. Instead: enforce caps and reject over-cap inputs before decoding (BE-244). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-BE-123 — Location data shipped.** Banned: publishing user photos with EXIF GPS coordinates intact by default. Defeats: DET-CODE-020. Instead: strip location metadata by default; any exception is a written product decision (BE-249). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-BE-124 — The lying progress state.** Banned: showing an asset as "ready," or animating a progress bar on a timer, before its processing job has actually completed. Defeats: DET-FAKE-022. Instead: read the state from the job record (BE-248). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-BE-121 — Golden-file test.** Verifies: BE-242, BE-245, BE-246. Check: automated — a fixed input set is processed in staging; assert every derivative matches the expected dimensions, formats, and duration, and that each carries a provenance row with source and recipe version. Pass: all match. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-BE-122 — Bomb-resistance test.** Verifies: BE-244. Check: automated in staging — submit a decompression-bomb fixture and an over-cap video; assert both are rejected within the resource limits and the worker is alive and processing normally afterward. Pass: rejected, worker healthy. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-BE-123 — Failure-state drill.** Verifies: BE-247, BE-248. Check: automated — submit a corrupt input that cannot transcode; assert the asset shows a failed state with a retry action and the raw original is not served at the derivative's URL. Pass: both hold. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-BE-124 — Metadata strip check.** Verifies: BE-243, BE-249. Check: automated — process a photo carrying GPS EXIF data; assert the published derivative contains no location tags. Pass: no GPS data present. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- Processing is a job, never a request.
- Nothing publishes from quarantine.
- Caps first: over-limit media is rejected, not attempted.
- Failure is a visible state with a retry, never a silent raw file.
- Every derivative can name its source and recipe.

## Checklist

- [ ] Processing runs from the queue; the upload request returns at quarantine (BE-241).
- [ ] Assets are unpublishable until their job succeeds (BE-242).
- [ ] Golden-file test green, provenance rows present (G-BE-121).
- [ ] Bomb and over-cap fixtures rejected, worker unharmed (G-BE-122).
- [ ] Forced failure shows a failed state; raw original not served (G-BE-123).
- [ ] Published photos carry no location metadata (G-BE-124).
- [ ] Rendition ladder is the documented one, not per-upload inventions (BE-245).

# notifications

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D4 Backend & APIs (BE)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Firebase Cloud Messaging documentation, https://firebase.google.com/docs/cloud-messaging
- **Depends on:** queues-jobs, api-building
- **Feeds into:** transactional-email (D11, email/SMS mechanics), admin-tools

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** a product event must reach a user — in-app inbox entries, push notifications (FCM/APNs, web push) — or when token handling, preferences, or dispatch reliability are in question.
- **Do NOT use when:** the channel is transactional email or SMS mechanics (sending infrastructure, templates, provider setup) — that is D11's transactional-email and sms skills, consumed through the same event. This skill owns push and in-app only.

## Rules

1. **BE-261 — Record first.** A domain event creates the notification record before anything is sent. The in-app inbox row is the source of truth; channel dispatch reads from it, never from the raw event alone.
2. **BE-262 — Dispatch from a queue.** Channel sends run as queued jobs. A provider call never executes synchronously inside the request or event that triggered the notification.
3. **BE-263 — Idempotent dispatch.** One event produces at most one notification per recipient per channel. Dispatch is keyed on the event ID, so retries and redeliveries cannot double-notify.
4. **BE-264 — Preferences at dispatch time.** Opt-outs and channel preferences are checked when the dispatch job runs, not when the event fires. A preference changed in between is honored.
5. **BE-265 — Every notification deep-links.** Each notification carries a link to the object it concerns. A notification that lands the user nowhere useful is unfinished work.
6. **BE-266 — Token lifecycle.** Device tokens are stored per user and per device. Tokens a provider reports as invalid are pruned on that feedback, tokens rotate on re-registration, and tokens are removed when a user logs out on a shared device.
7. **BE-267 — Sends leave records.** Every send records the provider's response (accepted, rejected, error) against the notification record. A send with no recorded outcome did not verifiably happen.
8. **BE-268 — Classes are written down.** Each notification type is classified as critical (security, billing) or ordinary. Critical types bypass marketing opt-outs but never a user's channel-blocking rights; the classification lives in one written table.
9. **BE-269 — Read state persists.** Inbox read and unread state is stored per user on the server and survives reloads and device changes.
10. **BE-270 — No staged content.** Inbox content is generated only by real events for that user. A new account's inbox is empty, apart from a clearly labeled welcome message.

## BAN list

- **BAN-BE-131 — The staged inbox.** Banned: rendering a hardcoded list of notifications that no real event generated. Defeats: DET-FAKE-013. Instead: records created by real events only; a new account starts empty (BE-261, BE-270). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-BE-132 — The in-request send.** Banned: calling a push or messaging provider synchronously inside the triggering request, with no queue and no failure path. Defeats: DET-CODE-006. Instead: write the record, enqueue dispatch, return (BE-261, BE-262). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-BE-133 — The double notify.** Banned: dispatch that can deliver the same event's notification more than once because sends are not keyed to the event. Defeats: DET-CODE-030. Instead: idempotency key of event ID + recipient + channel, checked before every send (BE-263). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-BE-134 — The immortal token.** Banned: ignoring provider invalid-token responses so dead tokens accumulate and send failures vanish unrecorded. Defeats: DET-CODE-005. Instead: record every provider response and prune invalid tokens on feedback (BE-266, BE-267). Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-BE-131 — Trigger test.** Verifies: BE-261, BE-263, BE-270. Check: automated — fire the triggering event on a test account; assert exactly one inbox row exists, exactly one dispatch per enabled channel, and that a freshly created account's inbox is empty. Pass: all assertions hold. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-BE-132 — Dead-token test.** Verifies: BE-266, BE-267. Check: automated — register a token, invalidate it at the provider, trigger a send; assert the failure is recorded with the provider response and the token is pruned. Pass: both hold. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-BE-133 — Preference timing test.** Verifies: BE-264, BE-268. Check: automated — fire an ordinary event, opt the user out before dispatch runs, and assert no send occurs; then fire a critical (security) event and assert it is still delivered. Pass: both hold. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-BE-134 — Device receipt check.** Verifies: BE-262. Check: scripted check on a test device or browser — trigger the event from a second session and confirm the push arrives while the triggering request has long finished. Pass: notification received on the device. Fail: block release of the notification feature. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- Record first, dispatch second — the inbox row is the truth.
- Sends run from a queue, never inside the triggering request.
- One event, one notification per recipient per channel.
- Preferences are read at dispatch time, not event time.
- Dead tokens are pruned on provider feedback, not eventually.

## Checklist

- [ ] Events create inbox records before any send (BE-261).
- [ ] Dispatch is queued and keyed on event ID (BE-262, BE-263).
- [ ] Trigger test green: one row, one send per channel, empty new inbox (G-BE-131).
- [ ] Invalid token pruned and its failure recorded (G-BE-132).
- [ ] Opt-out between event and dispatch is honored; critical class still sends (G-BE-133).
- [ ] Every notification deep-links to its object (BE-265).
- [ ] Classification table exists and covers every notification type (BE-268).

<!-- generated from skills/backend/queues-jobs/SKILL.md (bundle form) -->

# queues-jobs

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D4 Backend & APIs (BE)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** BullMQ production patterns — attempts, backoff, failed set as DLQ — https://railway.com/guides/bullmq-jobs-retry-dlq ; NestJS queue retries and dead-letter handling — https://soundscode.com/nestjs/nest-queue-retries
- **Depends on:** api-building, error-handling
- **Feeds into:** notifications, media-processing, realtime

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** work is slow, retryable, or owed to a third party — email, media processing, webhook delivery, provider calls, scheduled work — and a user request should not wait for it or lose it.
- **Do NOT use when:** the caller needs the result to answer the request; synchronous work that is fast and local stays in the handler. Do not use a queue to hide a missing retry policy — an unconfigured queue loses work more quietly than a function call, not less.

## Rules

1. **BE-181 — Slow or third-party work is a job.** Email, media processing, webhook delivery, and provider calls are enqueued, never executed inside the request that triggered them. The request returns; the worker owns delivery.
2. **BE-182 — Enqueue with the state change.** The job is enqueued in the same database transaction as the state change that causes it (transactional outbox where the store and the queue differ). A crash between the two loses neither.
3. **BE-183 — The retry policy is explicit.** Every job type declares max attempts and exponential backoff with jitter, and names which failures are permanent. The library default — commonly 1 attempt — is never accepted silently.
4. **BE-184 — Handlers are idempotent.** Delivery is at-least-once, so a handler can run twice for the same job with a single effect. The idempotency guard is part of the handler, not a hope about the queue.
5. **BE-185 — Payloads carry IDs.** A job payload holds record IDs and the handler re-reads the record at execution time. A payload that embeds the object acts on a stale snapshot.
6. **BE-186 — The dead-letter queue is a destination.** Exhausted jobs land in an inspectable failed set / DLQ that is alerted on and replayable by an operator. A job that vanishes after its last attempt is lost work.
7. **BE-187 — Permanent failures fail fast.** A failure class that cannot succeed on retry (bad address, provider 4xx) skips the remaining attempts and goes straight to the DLQ with its reason recorded.
8. **BE-188 — Recurring jobs register once.** Scheduled jobs are registered idempotently at deploy, so a redeploy never creates a duplicate schedule.
9. **BE-189 — Progress reads job state.** Any user-facing progress, sync, or "processing" indicator is read from the job's real state. No timer, estimate, or assumption renders as progress.
10. **BE-190 — Queues are monitored.** Queue depth and oldest-job age are metrics with alert thresholds. A growing queue is an incident, not a backlog to admire.
11. **BE-191 — Every job type has an owner.** Each registered job type names an owner, its max-attempts value, and its DLQ before it ships. An unregistered job type found in code fails review.

## BAN list

- **BAN-BE-091 — Fire-and-forget side effects.** Banned: calling the email, payment, or webhook provider inline or as an unawaited promise with no queue, so a crash or rejection silently drops the work. Defeats: DET-CODE-023. Instead: enqueue the job in the same transaction as the order (BE-182) and let the worker own delivery. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-BE-092 — Default-attempt jobs.** Banned: shipping a job type with the library's default attempt count and no backoff — choosing "lose the work" by omission. Defeats: DET-CODE-006. Instead: declare max attempts, exponential backoff with jitter, and the permanent-failure classes in the job's registration (BE-183). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-BE-093 — The unguarded handler.** Banned: a handler with no idempotency guard on its effect (charge, send, create), so at-least-once redelivery performs the effect twice. Defeats: DET-CODE-030. Instead: key the effect on the job's idempotency key or a unique constraint and check before acting (BE-184). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-BE-094 — Progress by stopwatch.** Banned: rendering "Processing… 80%" or "Sync complete" from elapsed time or a fixed script while the job is queued, failed, or never ran. Defeats: DET-FAKE-022. Instead: poll or stream the job's actual state and render only that (BE-189). Severity: BLOCK.

## Gates

- **G-BE-091 — Failure-injection test.** Verifies: BE-183, BE-184. Check: automated — in staging, kill the worker mid-job and make the provider fail the first two attempts; assert the job retries with backoff and the effect occurs exactly once. Local-harness form: where no staging environment exists, run the same drill against a local queue and worker processes — kill the local worker mid-job and make the local provider stub fail the first two attempts — under the same assertions, with the results recorded in progress.md; the staging form remains required before launch. Pass: one effect, job completed, attempts logged. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-BE-092 — DLQ drill.** Verifies: BE-186, BE-187. Check: automated — submit a job whose target permanently fails (an invalid recipient address); assert it fast-fails or exhausts into the DLQ, an alert fires, and an operator replay after the input is fixed succeeds. Local-harness form: where no staging environment exists, run the same drill against a local queue and worker processes with a permanently failing target, under the same assertions, with the results recorded in progress.md; the staging form remains required before launch. Pass: parked, alerted, replayable. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-BE-093 — Transactional-enqueue test.** Verifies: BE-182. Check: automated — in a test harness, force a crash at the commit boundary of a state change; then scan for orphans in both directions. Pass: no state change exists without its job, and no job without its state change. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-BE-094 — Registry audit.** Verifies: BE-188, BE-191. Check: automated — diff the job types referenced in code against the job registry, asserting each has an owner, max attempts, backoff, and DLQ; deploy twice and assert recurring registrations did not duplicate. Pass: full coverage, no duplicate schedules. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- Slow, retryable, or owed to a third party: it is a job.
- Enqueue in the same transaction as the state change.
- Delivery is at-least-once; handlers are idempotent.
- The library's default attempts is a decision — never accept it silently.
- Exhausted jobs park in the DLQ: alerted, inspectable, replayable.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every job type is registered with owner, max attempts, backoff, and DLQ (G-BE-094).
- [ ] Failure-injection test: exactly one effect after a mid-job kill and provider failures (G-BE-091).
- [ ] DLQ drill: the failed job is parked, alerted, and replayable (G-BE-092).
- [ ] No state change exists without its job, and no job without its state change (G-BE-093).
- [ ] Payloads carry IDs only; handlers re-read at execution time (BE-185).
- [ ] User-facing progress reads real job state (BE-189).
- [ ] Queue depth and oldest-job age have alert thresholds (BE-190).

# rate-limiting

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D4 Backend & APIs (BE)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** Stripe, "Rate limits", https://edge-docs.stripe.com/rate-limits ; OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023), API4 Unrestricted Resource Consumption, https://orca.security/resources/blog/owasp-api-security-top-10/
- **Depends on:** api-building, backend-auth
- **Feeds into:** api-documentation, sdk-design, monitoring (D12)

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** any endpoint is reachable by untrusted traffic — which is every public endpoint — and when setting or reviewing limits, limiter keys, expensive-operation caps, or 429 behavior.
- **Do NOT use when:** the limit in question is a provider's own quota imposed on the product from outside (that is capacity planning in D11's third-party-apis), or application-level fairness inside a job queue (queues-jobs owns job concurrency).

## Rules

1. **BE-301 — Limits per route class.** Limits are set per route class, not as one global guess: a generous per-account ceiling for ordinary reads, strict limits on authentication and other sensitive flows, and separate caps for expensive operations.
2. **BE-302 — Unspoofable keys.** Limiter keys derive from the authenticated account ID, or from a client IP verified through a trusted proxy chain. A forwarding header from an untrusted hop is never a key.
3. **BE-303 — Independent auth limits.** Login, signup, and password-reset endpoints carry their own per-account and per-IP limits, budgeted independently of general traffic, so credential stuffing cannot hide inside it.
4. **BE-304 — Bounded operations.** Every list, export, and search endpoint enforces a maximum page size and a query-cost ceiling. Requests above the maximum are clamped or rejected, never executed as asked.
5. **BE-305 — Concurrency caps on expensive work.** Search, export, AI calls, and upload processing carry an in-flight concurrency cap in addition to a rate, because their cost is concurrent load, not request count.
6. **BE-306 — The 429 contract.** A rejection returns 429 with a machine-readable body that names the limit that was hit and a `Retry-After` value. "Try again later" with no number is a contract violation.
7. **BE-307 — Metered downstream budgets.** Calls that cost money — SMS, email sends, paid third-party APIs — carry their own tighter per-account budgets, separate from compute limits.
8. **BE-308 — Limits are owned configuration.** Every limit value lives in configuration with a named owner and a review note. A numeric limit literal in handler code that nobody can explain is a defect.
9. **BE-309 — Good clients can survive.** The documented client behavior — honor `Retry-After`, back off exponentially with jitter — is published with the API, so legitimate clients ride out limits instead of amplifying them.
10. **BE-310 — Limit telemetry.** 429 counts are metered per route class and key type, and a sustained rise is alerted on. A limit silently rejecting real users is an incident discovered by telemetry, not by complaints.

## BAN list

- **BAN-BE-151 — The unbounded endpoint.** Banned: list, export, or search endpoints with no maximum page size or cost ceiling. Defeats: DET-CODE-033. Instead: clamp to the documented maximum and enforce a cost ceiling (BE-304). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-BE-152 — The spoofable key.** Banned: keying the limiter on a client-supplied forwarding header with no trusted proxy chain behind it. Defeats: DET-CODE-020. Instead: key on the authenticated account ID or a verified client IP (BE-302). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-BE-153 — Auth inside the general budget.** Banned: login and reset endpoints limited only by the global ceiling, with no per-account or per-IP limit of their own. Defeats: DET-CODE-033. Instead: independent, strict auth limits (BE-303). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-BE-154 — The magic-number limit.** Banned: rate limits buried as unexplained numeric literals in handler code, with no owner and no review note. Defeats: DET-CODE-009. Instead: named configuration with an owner (BE-308). Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-BE-151 — Burst test.** Verifies: BE-301, BE-303, BE-306. Check: automated — scripted traffic above each documented limit asserts 429 responses carrying `Retry-After` and the limit's name, while a second key and normal-rate traffic on the same routes pass unaffected. Pass: all assertions hold. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-BE-152 — Spoof test.** Verifies: BE-302. Check: automated — send requests with rotating forged `X-Forwarded-For` values from one real source; assert the caller's budget does not reset and the limit still engages. Pass: budget unchanged by forged headers. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-BE-153 — Bound scan.** Verifies: BE-304, BE-305. Check: automated — request every list, export, and search endpoint with extreme page-size and cost parameters; assert responses are clamped to the documented maxima and expensive routes refuse excess concurrency. Pass: all clamped. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-BE-154 — Limit config audit.** Verifies: BE-308. Check: automated grep plus config review — every limiter value resolves to a configuration entry carrying an owner; handler code contains no bare numeric limit literals. Pass: zero unexplained literals. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- Every endpoint is capped: rate, page size, cost, concurrency.
- Key on what the caller cannot forge.
- Auth gets its own stricter budget, always.
- 429 is a contract: name the limit, give a number, say when to retry.
- A limit nobody can explain is an outage or a hole.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every route class has a documented limit (BE-301).
- [ ] Burst test green: 429s carry the contract, other keys unaffected (G-BE-151).
- [ ] Forged forwarding headers do not reset any budget (G-BE-152).
- [ ] List, export, and search endpoints clamp to documented maxima (G-BE-153).
- [ ] Auth endpoints carry independent per-account and per-IP limits (BE-303).
- [ ] Metered downstream calls carry their own budgets (BE-307).
- [ ] All limit values live in owned configuration, no magic numbers (G-BE-154).

# rbac

## Metadata

- **Owner department:** D4 Backend & APIs (BE)
- **Skill version:** 1.0.0
- **Last verified:** 2026-11-21
- **Sources:** NIST CSRC, "Role Based Access Control" — https://csrc.nist.gov/projects/role-based-access-control ; OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023), API1/API5 — https://orca.security/resources/blog/owasp-api-security-top-10/
- **Depends on:** backend-auth, api-building
- **Feeds into:** admin-tools, user-reporting

## When to use / Do NOT use

- **Use when:** the product has more than one kind of user (member, moderator, staff, tenant admin) and any operation must be restricted by who is asking — which is to say, on every multi-role API, before the first protected route ships.
- **Do NOT use when:** the only question is *who* the caller is — that is backend-auth. RBAC starts after authentication, at the question of what this identity may do. Do not use a feature flag as a permission system; flags hide features, they do not authorize (see feature-flags).

## Rules

1. **BE-121 — Deny by default.** A route with no policy entry is unreachable, not open. Access exists only where the permission matrix grants it.
2. **BE-122 — Enforced on the server, per request.** Every protected operation runs its permission check inside the handler or in middleware bound to the route. UI visibility is presentation, never the check.
3. **BE-123 — Role comes from the server record.** The role that authorizes a request is read from the server-side session or user record. A role, flag, or header supplied by the client is ignored.
4. **BE-124 — Two checks, not one.** Function-level authorization (may this role call this operation at all — OWASP API5) and object-level authorization (may this identity act on this record — OWASP API1) are checked separately; passing one never implies the other.
5. **BE-125 — The matrix is a document.** The permission matrix (roles × operations) lives in the repo, and the authorization tests are generated from it. A route with no matrix row does not ship.
6. **BE-126 — Tenant scope is part of the check.** A role grants rights inside one tenant context only. Every check carries the tenant; an admin of tenant A has no rights in tenant B.
7. **BE-127 — Assignment is privileged and logged.** Granting or revoking a role is an admin-only operation, recorded in the audit log with actor, target, old role, new role, and timestamp.
8. **BE-128 — Denials are logged.** Every denied privileged attempt is recorded with actor, target, and timestamp. A silent denial hides an attack in progress.
9. **BE-129 — Roles are least-privilege sets.** Each role holds the minimum permissions its job needs. A catch-all admin role used for routine operations is a defect.
10. **BE-130 — Policy changes are code changes.** The matrix and the policy code change through the same review as code. There is no runtime role-editing path outside the audited assignment operation (BE-127).

## BAN list

- **BAN-BE-061 — Cosmetic permissions.** Banned: enforcing a permission only by hiding UI controls while the endpoint answers any authenticated caller. Defeats: DET-FAKE-021. Instead: check the permission server-side on every request and return 403. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-BE-062 — The client-stored admin flag.** Banned: treating a client-stored value (`isAdmin: true` in localStorage, a role field in the request body) as authorization evidence. Defeats: DET-FAKE-002. Instead: read the role from the server-side session record on every request (BE-123). Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-BE-063 — The unguarded new route.** Banned: shipping a route with no policy entry so it defaults to open. Defeats: DET-CODE-020 (nearest match — no DET parameter names this exact signal). Instead: deny-by-default policy table — the route returns 403 until a matrix row grants a role access. Severity: BLOCK.
- **BAN-BE-064 — The client copy decides.** Banned: implementing the permission rule in the frontend as the deciding copy while the server re-derives it with different conditions. Defeats: DET-CODE-027. Instead: the server is the only enforcement; the client mirrors the matrix for display and defers every decision to the server's response. Severity: WARN.

## Gates

- **G-BE-061 — Authorization matrix test.** Verifies: BE-121, BE-122, BE-124. Check: automated — the CI suite generated from the permission matrix requests every protected endpoint as each role, as an anonymous caller, and as a different user, asserting 401/403 and no record data in denied responses. Pass: every matrix cell matches its expected outcome. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-BE-062 — Cross-tenant access test.** Verifies: BE-126. Check: automated — seed two tenants; as tenant A's admin, attempt read, write, and delete on tenant B's records by direct ID. Pass: zero cross-tenant successes. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-BE-063 — Client-trust scan.** Verifies: BE-123. Check: automated — grep the API codebase for role or permission values read from request bodies, headers, or client storage (`isAdmin`, `req.body.role`, `req.headers['x-role']`); every hit is reviewed by hand. Pass: zero hits outside the server-side session-record lookup. Fail: block shipment until removed. Recorded in: progress.md.
- **G-BE-064 — Audit-log completeness check.** Verifies: BE-127, BE-128. Check: automated — in staging, perform one role grant and one denied admin attempt, then query the audit log for both. Pass: both records exist with actor, target, and timestamp. Fail: block shipment. Recorded in: progress.md.

## Recall anchors

- Deny by default: a route with no policy entry is closed.
- The server checks; the UI only hides.
- The authorizing role comes from the server record, never the request.
- Function-level and object-level are two different checks.
- Every grant and every denial lands in the audit log.

## Checklist

- [ ] The permission matrix is in the repo and every route has a row (BE-125).
- [ ] Matrix test passes for every role, including anonymous and other-user cells (G-BE-061).
- [ ] Cross-tenant test passes with zero successes (G-BE-062).
- [ ] No role is read from the request or client storage anywhere (G-BE-063).
- [ ] Role grants, revocations, and denied admin attempts appear in the audit log (G-BE-064).
- [ ] Roles are least-privilege sets; no routine catch-all admin (BE-129).
